syllabus.clause: carrying deletes into table formats via MERGE/delete files

sources.source: Debezium docs: event flattening (New Record State Extraction)

items.item: A database DELETE operation causes Debezium to generate two Kafka records: a record with op: d, the before row data; and a tombstone record with the same key and a null value, which is a marker for Apache Kafka indicating that log compaction can remove all records for that key
The drop mode removes both the DELETE event and the tombstone from the stream; the rewrite mode edits the record to add a __deleted: true field instead of dropping it

sources.source: Confluent docs: Kafka log compaction (standing in for an unreadable Apache Kafka page)

items.item: A message with a key and a null payload will be treated as a delete from the log
All delete markers for deleted records will be seen, provided the consumer reaches the head of the log in a time period less than the topic's delete.retention.ms setting (the default is 24 hours)
Since the removal of delete markers happens concurrently with reads, it is possible for a consumer to miss delete markers if it lags by more than delete.retention.ms
delete.enabled specifies whether the connector processes DELETE or tombstone events and removes the corresponding row from the database
A delete event's before field contains only the primary key column when the table's REPLICA IDENTITY setting is DEFAULT

at.step: Reveal: the before-image follows the identity

items.item: tombstones.on.delete controls whether a delete event is followed by a tombstone event

The before-image measurement runs the identical DELETE statement against the same table before and after an ALTER TABLE ... REPLICA IDENTITY change, isolating the identity setting as the only variable, rather than comparing two separately constructed tables that might differ in other ways too.

The soft-versus-hard measurement uses one single cursor query, run once, against a table holding both a soft-deleted and a hard-deleted row side by side, so the contrast is the same query's own two different outcomes rather than two separately worded queries that might behave differently for unrelated reasons.

The MERGE measurement applies one statement that simultaneously inserts, updates and deletes different rows in the same batch, confirming the delete clause doesn't accidentally touch the insert or update clauses' own rows, not merely that a delete-only batch works.

The compaction model's own _compact function is exercised twice against the identical input records, varying only the current time relative to the retention window, isolating timing as the sole variable between the correct and the resurrecting outcome.

The resurrection proof asserts the lagging consumer's own final state still contains the deleted key with its pre-delete value, not merely that the compacted log lacks a tombstone, which is the sharper, more specific claim CHAPTER.md's own hook requires.

The wrong option in the first predict question — that compaction keeps both of a delete's two records — is ruled out by definition: compaction's own rule, reproduced in _compact, keeps only the single latest offset per key, so the earlier record is structurally excluded regardless of retention timing.

The wrong option in the final predict question — that a source's own log retention is the number to size a sink's lag against — is ruled out by the measured retention-race proof itself: once a delete is already a tombstone in Kafka, the source's own retention no longer governs anything about that key.

Every scratch table, slot and temp table this topic creates is confirmed dropped inside the same function that created it, verified by three successive clean runs of examples.py, and the shared orders table (50001 rows) is never touched by any of this topic's four functions.
